iran-missile-strike-ceasefire-broken.headline: Iran fires missiles at Israel for first time since April ceasefire, shattering three-month truce
iran-missile-strike-ceasefire-broken.body_md:
Iran launched a volley of missiles at Israel on Monday, breaking a three-month ceasefire that had held since early April and reigniting the risk of wider Middle East conflict. The strike marks the first direct Iranian attack on Israeli territory since the truce took effect, potentially unraveling months of relative calm.

The breach carries immediate financial weight. Middle East escalation typically sends crude oil prices higher and triggers a broad risk-off in equity markets — vulnerabilities that had priced in the April ceasefire's stability premium. Investors will now weigh whether this is a singular breach or a precursor to sustained hostilities.

How Iran and Israel respond over the coming days will determine whether this becomes a turning point or a contained incident.

national-grid-ofgem-reopeners.headline: National Grid files 25 tactical proposals with Ofgem to reshape its multi-billion five-year investment plan
national-grid-ofgem-reopeners.body_md:
National Grid filed 25 transmission investment proposals with Ofgem on June 3, seeking regulatory approval for roughly £4.5 billion in new spending across England and Wales — a sum that, if cleared, would materially reshape the company's capital programme under the RIIO-T3 price control.

The filings were made under Ofgem's "re-openers" framework, a mechanism that allows network companies to revisit their funding arrangements mid-period when demand or network conditions have moved beyond the assumptions baked into the original price control settlement. For National Grid Electricity Transmission, the driver is clear enough: the energy system it was designed to serve when RIIO-T3 was set is not the one it operates today.

## What £4.5bn buys

The 25 proposals span connections for new low-carbon generation capacity, grid access for major industrial users and data centres, and reinforcements aimed at keeping pace with rising electricity demand. Grid connection delays have become, in the words of one assessment, "one of the biggest barriers to the delivery of clean energy projects" — a constraint that gives the submission political as well as commercial weight.

Rob Salter-Church, regulation director at National Grid Electricity Transmission, was direct about the impetus: "Britain's energy system is changing rapidly, and the transmission network must keep pace."

The £4.5 billion request sits inside a larger £70 billion, five-year investment envelope that National Grid has laid out across its UK and US operations. The re-openers process is, in effect, the mechanism by which that headline figure gets tested: each proposal must clear Ofgem's scrutiny on necessity, design, and cost-efficiency before funding is confirmed. Ambition on paper does not automatically translate into allowed expenditure.

Ofgem will now consult on the applications — a process that involves reviewing project justifications, soliciting third-party responses, and weighing consumer bill implications before issuing determinations. The regulator has signalled it expects investments to demonstrate long-term cost reduction and consumer value, language that puts the burden squarely on National Grid to show its spending is efficient, not merely large.

For NGG shareholders, the consultation represents a discrete earnings variable: if Ofgem disallows or scales back a material portion of the £4.5 billion, the company's return profile over the remaining RIIO-T3 period contracts accordingly. Full approval would validate National Grid's capital deployment strategy and underpin the dividend assumptions currently embedded in consensus forecasts. The company has not specified when it expects Ofgem to conclude its review, but National Grid's next results update will be the first formal venue to gauge how the regulator is receiving the filings.
national-grid-ofgem-reopeners.in_one_sentence: National Grid asked Ofgem to approve £4.5bn in additional transmission investment via 25 re-opener filings, with the regulator's verdict shaping NGG's return profile through the RIIO-T3 period.

centene-bofa-conviction-list.headline: BofA adds Centene to highest-conviction list as institutional consensus on managed care firms up
centene-bofa-conviction-list.body_md:
Bank of America handed Centene Corporation (NYSE: CNC) one of its more coveted designations on May 27, placing the managed care insurer on the firm's US 1 List — its highest-conviction roster of stocks expected to outperform. The move came a day after Barclays separately lifted its price target on Centene to $75 from $63, maintaining an Overweight rating and noting that share price moves across the managed care sector following first-quarter earnings "appear sustainable." The convergence was not coincidental.

Centene was already sitting on a notably broad institutional base. As of Q1 2026, 72 hedge funds held the stock — one of the widest ownership footprints in managed care — and it ranks among the top ten equities held by members of Congress. BofA's addition does not arrive at a blank slate; it reinforces a consensus already in formation. Notably, BofA made the change as a direct swap within managed care: at the same time Centene joined the US 1 List, Cigna was removed. That rotation signals a deliberate preference for government-program exposure over commercial book, particularly as inflationary pressures continue to compress commercial payer margins.

## The numbers that earned the call

Centene's Q1 2026 results gave analysts something concrete to act on. The company posted adjusted earnings per share of $3.37 — comfortably ahead of the $2.20–$2.30 consensus — on revenue of $49.94 billion, roughly $2.4 billion above forecasts. The headline beat mattered less than the trajectory underneath it. Consolidated health benefits ratio came in at 87.3%, with the Medicaid segment showing a 50-basis-point year-on-year improvement to 93.1%. That figure is the one investors had been watching.

Medicaid margins have been the central anxiety for managed care since 2023. The end of pandemic-era continuous enrollment protections triggered a wave of eligibility redeterminations that stripped membership and reset remaining beneficiaries toward higher-acuity, costlier patients. Centene, as the largest Medicaid managed care organization in the US, absorbed that pain at scale. The Q1 data suggests the worst is clearing.

CEO Sarah London told investors the quarter reflected "excellent progress within the Medicaid business," attributing gains to efforts to "modernize and standardize processes to better manage medical cost trend." Management raised full-year adjusted EPS guidance to above $3.40, up from the above-$3.00 floor set in February, and lifted premium and service revenue guidance by $1 billion to a $171–$175 billion range. Cash flow from operations for the quarter was $4.4 billion.

The forward question is straightforward: Centene's second-quarter results, expected in late July, will be the first test of whether Q1 momentum was structural or seasonal. A second consecutive improvement in Medicaid HBR would cement the thesis; any reversal would put the BofA conviction call under immediate pressure.
centene-bofa-conviction-list.in_one_sentence: BofA's US 1 List addition of Centene — paired with a Barclays price target raise and 72 hedge fund holders — marks a broad institutional bet on managed care's Medicaid recovery.

cms-community-health-fair-value-cut.headline: CMS reimbursement proposal forces analysts to trim Community Health Systems fair value
cms-community-health-fair-value-cut.body_md:
Community Health Systems, one of the larger for-profit hospital chains in the United States, is facing fresh scrutiny from Wall Street as a Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services proposal threatens to cap a revenue stream that has quietly grown into a material part of hospital balance sheets: Medicaid supplemental payments.

Simply Wall St. has revised its intrinsic value estimate for CHS (NYSE: CYH) from US$3.49 to US$3.31 per share — a modest 5% reduction, but one rooted in materially altered earnings assumptions. Revenue growth in the underlying model shifted from a projected +1.53% to a forecast contraction of 1.76%, while the net profit margin assumption collapsed from 5.39% to near-zero. Those are not incremental tweaks. The discount rate moved slightly higher, too, from 12.32% to 12.46%, reflecting a more cautious read on risk-adjusted returns in the sector.

## The Reimbursement Squeeze

At the centre of the concern is a proposed rule CMS published on 20 May 2026, which would cap Medicaid state-directed payments — often called supplemental payments — at 100% of Medicare rates in expansion states and 110% in non-expansion states. The vehicle for these payments has expanded sharply over the past decade: only two states used them in 2016; 41 now do, and CMS projects the pool would grow from US$107 billion in 2024 to US$296 billion by 2034 absent restriction. The agency estimates finalisng the rule as proposed would save the federal government more than US$510 billion over ten years.

For hospital operators, supplemental payments are not a rounding error. Industry analysts estimate they account for between 4% and 10% of revenue at major chains including HCA Healthcare, Tenet, and Universal Health Services. CHS itself disclosed approximately US$25 million in Q1 2026 from Georgia's Directed Payment Program — though management noted roughly half was offset by provider-tax increases in Indiana. The exposure is real, if partially hedged by state-level variation.

Analysts at Barclays and Truist moved first: each trimmed their CHS price targets by US$0.50, from US$3.50 to US$3.00, on the day the rule landed, with both maintaining neutral ratings. The Simply Wall St. fair-value revision arrived in the same window, and the directional consistency matters — more conservative revenue modelling, slightly higher discount rates, and a recognition that margins already under pressure have less policy cushion than previously assumed. CHS's Q1 2026 adjusted EBITDA fell 17.8% year-on-year to US$309 million, even as the company maintained its full-year EBITDA guidance of US$1.34 billion to US$1.49 billion.

The proposed rule is notable for extending beyond what the Republican-led "One Big Beautiful Bill" outlined in Congress. That congressional scope was already unsettling for the sector. That CMS's draft exceeds it is the added complication — and the one that analysts appear to be pricing for, however cautiously.

A 60-day public comment period is now under way. The American Hospital Association, the Federation of American Hospitals, and America's Essential Hospitals have each flagged concerns about access to care for underserved populations, arguing that supplemental payments compensate for chronically inadequate base Medicaid rates. CMS has countered that the growth in directed payments reflects cost-shifting and requires tighter alignment with Medicare benchmarks.

Whether those objections reshape the final rule has material implications for sector earnings across the board. The first concrete signal lands with CHS's Q2 2026 results, expected in late July, when management will face direct questions on guidance and how much of the proposed rule they have already baked in.

hallador-merom-turbine-coal-bet.headline: Hallador commits $350m to new coal turbines, betting Merom can outlast the energy transition
hallador-merom-turbine-coal-bet.body_md:
Hallador Energy, operator of a 1,080-megawatt coal-fired station on the Indiana side of the Wabash River, has agreed to pay $350 million for 460 megawatts of Siemens natural gas turbines it intends to install at the same site. The purchase agreement, announced June 1, marks the largest single capital commitment in the company's history and locks in equipment that management says gives the project its first realistic chance of advancing.

The turbines — acquired from Australia-based Energy World Corporation, never previously fired — carry a headline price of roughly $760 per kilowatt. Delivering them to the Merom site in Sullivan County adds approximately $100 million in transportation, refurbishment, and logistics, pushing the total delivered cost to around $450 million. That figure represents more than half of the estimated total project cost. CEO Brent Bilsland was direct about why the company moved when it did. "Until you have equipment, you don't have a project," he said at the announcement. "We now have Siemens equipment — at what we believe is the right price, at the right time."

The pricing rationale is straightforward: new turbine order books at major manufacturers currently stretch years into the future. Acquiring never-fired units on the secondary market short-circuits that queue, and Hallador argues it did so at a discount to new-build alternatives.

## Not quite the coal bet it looks like

Hallador sits awkwardly in the coal-stock column. It owns the Oaktown underground mines in Knox and Sullivan counties, and Merom's two generating units still burn bituminous coal. But the turbine purchase is for a proposed natural gas combustion turbine project at the site — additional capacity alongside the existing coal plant, not a coal retrofit. Hedge funds holding approximately $118 million in HNRG as of the first quarter of 2026 are, in effect, making a bet on gas-fired capacity demand as much as on coal's staying power.

What keeps the stock interesting to those funds is Hallador's contracted position. The company's sales book exceeded $2.1 billion in 2026, anchored by a 12-year capacity agreement running 2028 to 2040 and valued at over $1 billion — priced at roughly $470 per megawatt-day, more than double the most recent capacity market clearing price of around $230 per megawatt-day. Jefferies upgraded the stock to Buy in March with a $22.50 price target, noting that Hallador deliberately left its Fall 2028 capacity uncontracted — a gap analysts read as space reserved for a potential deal with a hyperscaler seeking reliable power for AI data centres.

The company enters this commitment from a clean balance sheet. It held no outstanding bank debt as of March 31, with a $120 million credit facility undrawn.

The turbine purchase does not trigger automatic construction. Hallador has set out a four-step path: secure equipment (done), enter MISO's ERAS interconnection study (imminent), market the power output under long-term purchase agreements (ongoing), and take a final investment decision only after the MISO study concludes — an outcome expected around September 2026. The company retains the option to build, sell the project with its new equipment, or sell the turbines independently.

If everything falls into place, commercial operations would begin between late 2028 and mid-2029. The September interconnection result is the next hard checkpoint — the moment when Hallador's three exit options stop being theoretical.

barclays-entergy-price-target-trim.headline: Barclays clips Entergy price target to $119 while holding its overweight on the regulated utility
barclays-entergy-price-target-trim.body_md:
Barclays' equity desk made a quiet housekeeping adjustment to its Entergy Corp. (NYSE: ETR) model on June 3, trimming the price target by five dollars — from $124 to $119 — while keeping its Overweight rating unchanged. The action drew little market fanfare, which is appropriate: at a 4% reduction with no accompanying rating move, it is the kind of recalibration that signals model upkeep rather than thesis revision.

The revised target sits roughly three dollars above the Street consensus of around $116, based on an average across seventeen analyst estimates, and still implies meaningful upside from ETR's recent trading range in the low-to-mid $110s.

## A soft patch since Q1

The timing points to first-quarter results as the proximate cause. Entergy reported adjusted EPS of $0.86 for Q1 2026 — a period Barclays later described as producing "lackluster" stock performance despite industrial sales growth of 15% year over year, buoyed by rising data-centre load. The headline print came in below some market expectations, and shares have lagged since.

Barclays did not retreat on the fundamental view. The bank described Entergy shares as "undervalued" and said they "provide strong value at the current level" — language that indicates a firm recalibrating its model rather than its conviction. For comparison: Truist made a similar incremental move on May 29, lowering its target from $130 to $127 while maintaining a Buy rating.

Entergy operates five regulated vertically integrated utilities across Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, and Texas, serving roughly three million customers from a generation mix spanning gas, nuclear, hydro, solar, and coal. Regulated utilities rarely prompt dramatic analyst pivots — rate cases, capital plans, and load growth are the levers, and they turn slowly.

![Entergy's New Orleans headquarters tower in the city's Central Business District](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/28/New_Orleans%2C_Louisiana_%2C_Entergy_building_from_Hilton_New_Orleans.JPG)

The forward story centres on Entergy's $57 billion, four-year capital programme, a plan enlarged substantially by a March agreement with Meta Platforms for a Louisiana data-centre campus requiring an estimated $15 billion in infrastructure investment. Management raised its 2029 adjusted EPS target to $6.40, projecting 12% growth in 2030, and still sees a pipeline of seven to twelve gigawatts of potential data-centre load sitting outside the current plan.

## June 9 as the next read

The more significant near-term event is Entergy's 2026 Investor Day, scheduled for June 9 in New York City. CEO Drew Marsh and the executive team are set to lay out the company's growth roadmap through 2030. Presentation materials will be posted before market open; a live webcast begins at 1 p.m. ET.

Barclays flagged the event explicitly as a positive catalyst — a signal that the bank expects updated load commitments or a refreshed capital plan to close the gap between the current share price and its revised $119 target. The Investor Day will provide the first formal look at whether management can translate a 7-to-12 GW data-centre pipeline into hard numbers. That is the figure to watch on Monday afternoon.

barclays-ai-tech-consolidation-warning.headline: Barclays warns of consolidation risk as the AI trade grows crowded
barclays-ai-tech-consolidation-warning.body_md:
Barclays strategists are cautioning that the powerful rally driven by artificial intelligence themes in semiconductor and technology stocks may be approaching a period of consolidation — though the warning arrives with less ammunition than traders looking for a clear exit signal might want.

The note, from a team led by European equity strategist Emmanuel Cau, is anchored in one genuinely striking data point: the MSCI World Semiconductors index has climbed roughly 50% in just two months. That is the second-strongest two-month performance recorded in that index since November 2001 — a period most investors would prefer not to treat as a benchmark. Cau's team stops short of turning outright bearish. Their message is more precise: the trade has become crowded, and June's calendar provides the kind of friction that can tip crowded positions into an unwind.

## What they're pointing at

The specific risks Barclays identifies are more substantive than standard elevated-valuation hedging. Hedge fund and commodity trading adviser positioning in AI and momentum names is described as extended, with systematic traders nearing the limits of their capacity to add. A wave of technology-sector IPOs and fresh capital raisings expected over the next few weeks will compete for the same pool of money that drove the advance. June is also unusually dense with macro events — chief among them the Federal Reserve's June 17 meeting, the first to be chaired by Kevin Warsh, alongside an expected European Central Bank rate decision.

Barclays also flags a structural concentration problem that sits one level beneath the headline index. Samsung and SK Hynix together account for more than half of South Korea's Kospi. TSMC alone represents 42% of Taiwan's TAIEX. A rotation out of chip names does not stay tidy; it lands hard on the indices where those names live.

"The combination of frothy technicals and a catalyst-heavy June suggests chances of a tactical pullback cannot be dismissed," Cau's team writes. The disclaimer follows in the same breath: "We are not bearish Semis."

## The limits of the warning

What the note does not provide is the underlying data that would convert caution into a signal. There are no published positioning ratios, no fund-flow figures, no valuation thresholds at which the strategists expect systematic selling to kick in. The CTA-extension claim is asserted rather than quantified. That omission matters: crowded trades have a well-documented habit of staying crowded — and generating further returns — until a specific catalyst forces the unwind rather than a general observation that one might arrive.

Barclays retains its broadly constructive view on equities, citing resilient corporate earnings and what it frames as a durable AI investment supercycle. In the event that semiconductor shares do pause, the suggested rotation destinations are familiar: software, aerospace and defence, and consumer discretionary sectors including luxury goods and travel. European markets are flagged as potential beneficiaries too.

The June 17 FOMC meeting is the next concrete test. Kevin Warsh's debut in the chair, against a backdrop of sticky inflation and elevated oil prices, will do more to clarify the macro foundation beneath the AI trade than any strategist note published this side of it.

musk-asml-spacex-terafab-pitch.headline: Musk hails ASML as Europe's greatest company ahead of SpaceX Terafab manufacturing pitch
musk-asml-spacex-terafab-pitch.body_md:
Elon Musk took to X on Saturday to call ASML "arguably the greatest company in Europe," adding that it "should be treasured and supported." The comment arrived ahead of a closed virtual discussion he is scheduled to hold this week with ASML chief executive Christophe Fouquet at the Dutch company's annual technology conference — an event restricted to employees and partners.

The venue is not incidental. ASML, headquartered in Veldhoven in the southern Netherlands, holds what amounts to a manufacturing monopoly on extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines — bus-sized devices that use precisely focused light to etch transistors at the nanometre scale onto silicon wafers. No other company makes them. Without EUV, it is effectively impossible to produce the most advanced chips that AI workloads depend on.

Musk's appearance at the conference is billed around SpaceX's Terafab concept, the company's plan to build a network of giant semiconductor fabrication complexes in Grimes County, Texas. The project — a three-way venture with Tesla and xAI, with Intel contributing its 14A process node — carries a reported initial price tag of $55 billion and a full build-out cost of up to $119 billion. Eighty percent of Terafab's projected output is earmarked for radiation-hardened chips destined for SpaceX's planned orbital satellite data centres: servers in low Earth orbit, running on solar power.

Musk himself has distilled the logic bluntly: "We either build the Terafab, or we don't have the chips, and we need the chips, so we build the Terafab."

## Flattery with a purpose

The praise sits in an obvious strategic context. Any leading-edge chip facility on the scale Musk is describing would require EUV machines by the dozen — which means ASML is, for practical purposes, indispensable to the Terafab roadmap. Courting the company's workforce and leadership before pitching the vision in detail is straightforward positioning.

What the announcement does not contain is any formal agreement, supply contract, or partnership announcement. The Benzinga report that first surfaced the exchange carries no figures on machine orders, delivery timelines, or financing arrangements between SpaceX and ASML. The discussion this week remains private, and the conference is not open to press.

ASML's machines currently run at roughly $380 million apiece for the most advanced high-NA EUV models. A fab at Terafab's projected scale would represent one of the largest single customers the Dutch company has ever seen — which makes Musk's praise feel less like an editorial opinion and more like a warm-up act.

The week's discussion will say little publicly; the conference releases no transcripts. What would move the needle is evidence of a supply agreement, a construction permit for the Grimes County site, or an update on the SpaceX IPO process — currently pricing the company at an implied $1.75 trillion. Until then, this is executive flattery with a legible motive, not a supply-chain shift.

international-dividend-yield-gap.headline: Why passive-income investors are looking abroad as US yields fail to clear 5.4%
international-dividend-yield-gap.body_md:
For a generation of income investors who built strategies around dividend reinvestment and passive cash flow, the arithmetic has quietly turned hostile. Generating $19,000 a year from a $350,000 portfolio requires a blended yield of 5.4%. The S&P 500, now yielding around 1.07% — a level not seen since the nineteenth century — offers no route to that number on its own.

The solution that a growing number of systematic income strategies have landed on is uncomfortable but logical: go international.

## The Numbers Demand It

The math is unforgiving. An equal-weighted basket of five heavily traded international names — British American Tobacco, HSBC, Shell, Novartis, and BHP — produces a blended yield of roughly 3.8%, generating about $13,300 on that same $350,000. Better than the S&P 500 by a multiple, but still $5,700 short of the target.

To close the gap, allocation has to do some work. Tilting 35% of the portfolio toward British American Tobacco (BTI), which currently yields 5.5% on an annualised payout of $3.34, and 25% toward HSBC — which paid $3.30 in dividends in 2025 and has guided to a 50% payout ratio through 2028 — gets the blended rate past 5.4%. Shell (3.6%) and Novartis (3.3%), which has raised its annual dividend from $3.38 in 2021 to $4.77 this year, fill out the growth component. BHP (2.9%) brings commodity exposure but drags the average; position sizing matters here.

The contrast with home markets is stark. Per Siblis Research, US equities yield 1.18% against 3.10% in the UK, 2.94% in France, and 4.45% in Italy. JPMorgan estimates US equities carry a 34% valuation premium over international peers — against a 19% long-run average — while the dollar sits roughly 10% above fair value. Both factors argue for the rotation.

There is a tax wrinkle worth naming. Foreign dividends typically attract a 15% withholding at source. In taxable accounts, the shortfall is reclaimable via IRS Form 1116's foreign tax credit; in tax-deferred accounts — IRAs and 401(k)s — the credit is forfeit. The after-tax yield in sheltered accounts is therefore lower than the headline rate, which matters when the target is already a squeeze.

What changes the calculus from here is currency. The yield advantage from international holdings comes partly from the weak dollar and partly from genuine payout culture differences — UK, Australian, and continental European companies have historically distributed higher fractions of earnings than their US counterparts. If the dollar claws back its overvaluation, some of the income gains get eaten at the exchange desk. The cleaner long-term watch is whether US large-cap payout ratios respond to any rotation out of buybacks — but there is no near-term catalyst. Until then, the 5.4% target points overseas.

floor.headline: Early exits preserved gains—and capped them
floor.body_md: Three names—LSEG, CLX, WELL—powered the day with midday take-profits of 8.5%, 4.9%, and 4.8%, combining for £458 of the £772 total. That early discipline locked in reversals, a cleaner read of mean reversion than the numbers alone suggest. But LSEG hinted at the limits of the thesis: an 8.57% intraday swing in a large-cap almost certainly involved news or order-flow beyond pure technicals, and the bot exited early enough to leave gains unrealized. Meanwhile, KPN, BTI, and BMW flatlined at scheduled exit—the exhaustion signal never confirmed, indicating the sell-side pressure was light rather than spent. Today looked disciplined. Tomorrow's opening will test whether that caution prevented disaster or simply capped opportunity.

floor.headline: The Momentum That Wasn't There
floor.body_md:
The strategy was clean: buy yesterday's strongest movers, let them run. Today it failed completely. All nine positions exited as losers—a £1,776 loss with no winners to offset. The thesis wasn't flawed so much as already exhausted by market open.

BRSHF, a foreign OTC share, carried the damage: £1,467 of the total. It had spiked +100% the prior session on what appears to have been a thin-market print; by morning's open, no follow-through materialized. MAC.L and ICON.L repeated the pattern: yesterday's 82% climbs had run their course. Scheduled exits meant holding dead thesis to market.

This is momentum exhaustion in textbook form: catching yesterday's winners, not tomorrow's. Whether tighter liquidity filters or confirmation requirements can prevent the same trap will emerge in the coming sessions.

floor.headline: Commodity momentum shines; quieter tier falters
floor.body_md: Commodity-momentum picked up the day's only win among quieter movers, posting £50.09 in gains (1.46% average) across INDU.L and NGSP.L. The rest struggled through choppy waters. News-reactive, momentum-trader-vix-gated, pair-rotator, and sector-rotator-factor-momentum all posted losses of £15–£25, each with flat 0.00% average returns, while bond-cycle managed just one losing trade (£25). The pattern signals indecisive markets where factor-based and rotational strategies found scant conviction—a day of modest attrition for the quieter tier.

floor.headline: TPL +9.7%, LITE −8.9%: excluded by universe boundaries
floor.body_md: The week's biggest movers landed at opposite extremes. TPL surged 9.69% with no identified catalyst. LITE fell 8.86% following Lululemon's guidance cut—both outside configured universes. MRNA (+7.49%) rallied on ASCO melanoma vaccine data showing 49% recurrence-risk reduction; the June 1 abstract front-ran post-close signals and sits outside biotech coverage. SNDK (+6.71%) caught semiconductor sector bounce but hit configured price-cap, spinoff-history, and RSI-ceiling thresholds. FDXF (+6.26%), spun June 1, had four sessions of trading—too brief for momentum lookbacks. All five exclusions flowed from universe scope: price ceilings, minimum history, sector boundaries. Configuration gaps explain the week's biggest misses.
